nuevo:
Rachel and John are proud new parents of a baby boy, Eli, but parenthood proves hard: six months on, Rachel is a sleep-deprived wreck and Eli is a fussy baby who cries constantly. In a box of baby things sent by her mother, which once belonged to Vivian, who lost both her baby, Zachary, and her husband under strange circumstances, Rachel finds an old book illustrated with demons and monsters that contains a lullaby. Out of desperation she sings it, and Eli miraculously falls asleep, so that at first the song seems a blessing. Soon, however, the couple hear voices and see strange things on the baby monitor, and Rachel glimpses an evil crone that seems to threaten her son. She visits Vivian in a mental institution and learns that her sister went through the same experience before losing her child, while John consults a tattooed rabbi who tells him of other ways to protect Eli. The lullaby, it emerges, has summoned the ancient demon Lilith, a taker of children served by her own deformed offspring, and the parents must face her to save their son.

The film was released on video on demand and digital platforms by Vertical in December 2022. Critics found it competent but formulaic. Jeffrey M. Anderson of Combustible Celluloid gave it two stars out of four, crediting committed performances and effective set design while calling the story all too familiar and its use of Jewish culture a checklist of terms. Jim Morazzini of Nerdly gave it two out of five, praising its dark, atmospheric look and its treatment of the stresses of new parenthood, but criticizing recycled jump scares and unconvincing computer effects. Kat Hughes of Ghouls Magazine was more positive, praising Chaplin's quiet strength and the film's place in the growing field of Jewish horror, and calling it one of Leonetti's strongest efforts as a director.

The original Larva shorts followed the urban misadventures of two grubs, the small, short-tempered Red and his bigger, dimmer best friend Yellow, neither of whom speaks a human language. Larva Island moved them to a tiny deserted island shared with Chuck, a shipwreck survivor. In the movie, Chuck is back home in New York City, where he nearly steps on a dung beetle but spares it because of the friends he once had among such creatures. Over a meal at a restaurant, he recounts his outlandish survival story to Grace, a reporter who wants to publish it, though he worries that nobody will believe him. His recollections trigger flashbacks to his time on the island: hunger and loneliness, repeated failures to build boats and rafts, storms, freezing cold, scorching heat, typhoons, a volcanic eruption and icebergs. He tells of how he survived thanks to Red and Yellow, whose antics included Red's rivalry for the affection of a female larva and Yellow's endless flatulence, and of other island companions such as Clara, a trained seal who washed ashore, and a tiny alien who took over the body of a crab to become a robotic "Crabsformer". Gradually, the whole restaurant becomes captivated by his stories, and the film adds a sentimental coda to Chuck's arc.

Much of the film consists of footage repurposed from episodes of the series, linked by new framing scenes, and critics were unimpressed. John Serba of Decider advised viewers to skip it, calling it a clip show disguised as a sequel whose relentless fart jokes become an endurance test, while conceding that its animation is simple and colorful. Bob Hoose of Plugged In described it as a poor man's Minions aimed at very young children, noting its mild messages about friendship and seeing things from another's point of view.

The story is set in a future devastated by a global pandemic worse than any before it and by climate change, where overpopulation and global warming have left resources desperately scarce and food shortages afflict the survivors. A totalitarian government known as the Bureau has introduced the "Deal" as its answer to the crisis: anyone who accepts it by their twentieth birthday is guaranteed work, shelter and everything they need to survive, but only for twenty more years, after which they are put to death to make room for others. Tala Bayani (Montano), a mother who took the Deal, is approaching the end of her term before she has managed to secure the survival of her daughter Analyn (Fischer), who suffers from kidney disease. With her time running out, Tala begins to fight back against the regime to save her child, and the two women find themselves trapped and racing to find a way out.

In an interview with the magazine Positively Filipino, Montano said that she modelled Tala on her own Filipina mother, Linda Montano, and the sacrifices she made in raising her as a single parent; the article described the mother-daughter relationship as the emotional centre of the film, taking precedence over its computer-generated cityscapes. Reviewing it for Week99er, Becky found that the premise of a pandemic followed by food shortages felt uncomfortably close to contemporary reality, but said the film held the attention with an interesting story and a couple of unexpected twists, and was relieved that its ending was less dark than she had anticipated, though some threads were left open. The German film magazine Filmdienst was less impressed, judging that the film failed to exploit the dramatic potential of its premise and settled into a thriller plot rendered rather pale, partly because of its low budget.

Built from newly filmed interviews with the cast and the series' executive producers, intercut with clips from the most pivotal moments of the first six seasons, the special has the actors tell the stories of their own characters from the moment each was introduced to where they stood at the end of the previous season. The story is retold season by season, beginning with the moment sheriff's deputy Rick Grimes, played by Andrew Lincoln, wakes from a coma in a Georgia hospital to find the world overrun by flesh-eating walkers, and searches for his wife Lori, his son Carl and his partner Shane. The retrospective then traces the group's path through the Atlanta camp and the Centers for Disease Control, Hershel Greene's farm and the fatal rivalry between Rick and Shane, the fortified prison and the war with the Governor of Woodbury, the scattering of the survivors and the trap of Terminus, and the move to the walled Virginia community of Alexandria. It ends with the conflict with the Saviors and their leader Negan, culminating in the first brutal swing of Negan's bat in the sixth-season finale, recounted by Jeffrey Dean Morgan and other members of the cast. The special was designed both to give viewers who had never seen an episode a chance to catch up on the plot, characters, locations and unique terminology of the series, and to offer devoted fans a refresher course before the new season.

The Walking Dead was then AMC's flagship series and a ratings phenomenon, executive produced by Kirkman, showrunner Scott M. Gimple, Gale Anne Hurd, David Alpert, Greg Nicotero and Tom Luse. The special served as the lead-in to a seventh season in which the survivors, fractured and bereaved after Negan's brutal example, would be forced to live under his rule.

Kai Kahale (Dacascos), a middle-aged Hawaiian former soldier, flies into Bangkok and orders a cab through an app. The driver is Fha (Golten), a young Anglo-Thai woman, and he offers her 6,000 dollars to drive him around the city all night without asking questions. His first stop is a law firm, where he shoots a lawyer in her office; the second is the apartment of a police officer, whom he kills with the words "This is for Lisa." As the bodies are discovered, an offbeat detective begins piecing together the string of killings. Over food at a roadside stall, Kai tells Fha that his daughter, her husband and their little girl died in a crash in Thailand and that he wants to meet everyone involved; shaken, Fha confesses that she too was involved in an accident in which a child died. After shooting a young man at a nightclub for destroying a family with his Porsche, Kai admits that he knows the car in the crash was hers and that he chose her as his driver on purpose, but that he will not kill her, preferring to let her live with her guilt. At a hospital he kills the wealthy gallery owner Davies (Boonthanakit), who had bribed the police to falsify reports and protect his son, along with his wife, bodyguard and son, and is wounded escaping in a doctor's disguise. Fha admits that she lied about the accident out of fear of the boy's father and used the money she received to pay for her sick brother's treatment. Kai offers her his bitcoins should he not return from his final target, a Japanese fixer with underworld ties (Kosugi). After defeating the fixer's men, a weakened Kai loses their hand-to-hand fight, but the detective arrives in time to shoot the fixer, and Kai insists that Fha was his hostage, not his accomplice. As she drives him to hospital, he loses consciousness.

John-John, known as JJ, is the son of a single immigrant mother and grows up in a working-class housing estate in Stockholm, surrounded by a multicultural group of friends led by his downstairs neighbor Sluggo, whose gang drifts into burglary and petty crime; his mother's boyfriend, a security guard, warns that they will all end up behind bars. Elisabeth lives in a seaside villa with her wealthy father and younger sister Patricia and is withdrawn and sarcastic, still grieving the death of her mother. Their worlds collide when JJ, out on a joyride in a stolen boat with Sluggo, rescues Patricia from drowning. Both are then admitted to the same performing arts school, and a slow, hesitant courtship develops as they rehearse for a school performance, explore the city and meet each other's friends, while hiding the relationship from her disapproving father. Sluggo's crimes, which include breaking into Elisabeth's home, increasingly entangle JJ, and when he is backed into a corner with no way out, the gulf between their lives threatens to tear the couple apart in a dark final act.

JJ+E premiered on Netflix on 8 September 2021. Critical reception was mixed. Decider's Jade Budowski praised its grounded portrait of Stockholm, the chemistry of the leads and the star quality of Elsa Öhrn, but felt the film wavered between romance and crime story before taking an absurd turn in its last minutes. Roger Moore of Movie Nation found the courtship scenes the strongest and valued its depiction of Sweden's multicultural underclass, yet called the surrounding melodrama a collection of clichés and the whole a formulaic, tepid teen romance.

Maggie Quinn (Hall) and Jack Russo (Williams), best friends since childhood, host Windy City Wake-Up, a morning radio show known for its relationship advice. When an on-air chat about introducing their partners to their families becomes a hit, their producer Deb (Brooks) tells them that a larger network, run by Judd Crawford (Dillon), wants to syndicate them nationally, provided they introduce their partners live during a New Year's Eve broadcast. Jack proposes holding the event at the Magnolia, the struggling restaurant and jazz club co-owned by their fathers Steve (Cumyn) and Martin (Shore). Days after Christmas, however, both are dumped, Maggie by her boyfriend Seb (Sean Williams). To save the opportunity, Jack suggests they pretend to be a couple. When Jack's parents catch them in a staged kiss, both families are overjoyed, having long believed they belonged together. Maggie's sister Amanda (Maria) sees that Maggie has always loved Jack, and Steve hands Jack the ring of Maggie's late mother. Jack's high-school girlfriend Bianca Bell (Gordon) tells him that Maggie was heartbroken when he did not take her to the prom, and that she broke up with him because he loved Maggie. After Jack forgets a dinner marking the anniversary of her mother's death, Maggie tells him he always puts her second. At the party Judd floats the idea of giving them separate shows, and as midnight approaches the pair confess on air that the relationship was a sham. Maggie leaves the stage, but Jack declares his love, turns down a solo show and sings a song he wrote for her, and they share a real midnight kiss. A year later he proposes with her mother's ring.

Reviews were mixed. Kirsten Hawkes of Parent Previews gave it a B+, finding Hall and Williams charming enough to carry an unremarkable script, while Roger Moore of Movie Nation called it as bland as bargain-shelf white bread and lamented the leads' lack of chemistry. It was nominated for Best TV Movie at the 2022 Canadian Screen Awards.

Sixteen-year-old Hendrik (Orlandianyi) moves with his mother Sabine (Koschitz) and his eight-year-old brother Eddi (Rosskopf) from Hanover to Bad Eisenkappel in Carinthia, where Sabine has taken a job at the Obir dripstone caves. The move is also meant to help the family cope with the father's death in an accident. For Hendrik it is a culture shock: the locals speak a dialect he can barely understand, and something seems wrong with the run-down house that estate agent Gerold Röckl (Michael Pink) found for them. Eddi starts sleepwalking and speaking Slovene, Hendrik is plagued by nightmares, and their mother grows increasingly desperate. After a difficult start the brothers make friends with the bold Ida (Marii Weichsler) and the nerdy Fritz (Lars Bitterlich), and the four set out to uncover the secret of the house.

The film departs from the book in several ways: the brothers were made older, they arrive with their widowed mother rather than both parents, and because the setting moved from the Allgäu to Carinthia, Slovene replaced the novel's Romanian. It was shot over 34 days in the summer of 2019 in Vienna and southern Carinthia. Following a premiere at the Wildenstein waterfall in Gallizien in September 2020 and a screening at Vienna's SLASH festival, it opened in Austrian cinemas on 30 October 2020 and reached Netflix in May 2021, where it entered the top ten in more than 50 countries.

Germany's film rating agency FBW gave it the rating "particularly valuable", praising suspense that goes well beyond typical children's adventures and a well-timed horror effect. Christian Klosz of Film plus Kritik commended its story, witty dialogue and the culture clash between the city family and local Carinthian colour, and The New York Times called it an effective family horror film. It won the audience award for best youth film at the Goldener Spatz and earned four Austrian Film Award nominations, including for Koschitz and Pink.

In the three months since Alberto Falcone's death, the Holiday killer has struck the Falcone and Maroni crime families on Valentine's Day, Saint Patrick's Day and April Fools' Day, while Bruce, under Poison Ivy's control, has signed many of his assets over to Falcone until Catwoman rescues him. Scarecrow's fear toxin forces Batman to relive his parents' deaths, and Bruce recalls how his father once saved Falcone's life. After Holiday kills Luigi Maroni on Father's Day, Sal Maroni offers to testify against Falcone, and Batman later finds Holiday's guns in the Dents' basement. In court, Maroni accuses Harvey of being Holiday and throws acid in his face. Disfigured, Harvey escapes from a trap set by Falcone's men and finds refuge in the sewers with Solomon Grundy. Batman learns that Catwoman is Falcone's daughter, while Harvey, now calling himself Two-Face, frees inmates from Arkham Asylum and leads an assault on Falcone's building, killing the mob boss, whose daughter Sofia also dies. Two-Face surrenders, claiming responsibility for the murders, but Batman confronts Gilda, the woman Alberto once loved, and discovers she is the true killer, driven by hatred of Falcone.

Batman: The Long Halloween was announced in August 2020 at DC FanDome, and its voice cast was revealed in March 2021. Part One was released in June 2021; Part Two was made available on digital platforms on 27 July 2021 and on DVD and Blu-ray on 10 August, and a deluxe edition combining both parts followed in September 2022. Critics praised it as a satisfying conclusion: ComicBookMovie and IGN commended its epic resolution and the way it wrapped up the main plot threads, CBR lauded its dynamic portrayal of DC's villains and strong character development.

The special was released during the long gap between the first and second seasons, when production of the second season had been halted by the COVID-19 pandemic, and it revisits the making of the first. Netflix promoted it as a journey into the world of the show, from the casting of the main roles to the bard Jaskier's catchy song "Toss a Coin to Your Witcher", and as a look behind the monsters, the ballads and the magic that went into bringing the Continent to the screen. Across its half-hour running time it touches on the history of the Continent and the first season's non-linear timeline, the relationships between Geralt of Rivia, Yennefer and Ciri, the show's magic system, the importance of the property in Poland, and the series' portrayal of women, with Chalotra praising Sapkowski's complex female characters. It also covers the design of the creatures, built through a combination of practical effects and computer-generated imagery, as well as costume and set design and their architectural influences, the fight choreography, and the experiences of the episode writers, among them Declan de Barra, who wrote the fourth episode, "Of Banquets, Bastards and Burials". The actors also discuss how they approached their characters, frequently complimenting one another's work.

Reception was mixed. Writing for FilmObserver, a self-described devoted fan of the franchise found the special rushed and more like an extended commercial than a documentary, arguing that it tried to cram far too many subjects into 30 minutes and lingered on familiar backstory at the expense of genuine behind-the-scenes material. The reviewer nonetheless enjoyed the too-brief segments on monster creation, costume and set design, which offered real production footage rather than clips from the show, as well as de Barra's insights and the actors' interviews.

The documentary centres on Valentine's Day, one of the biggest nights in the club's calendar. Behind the scenes, the 78-year-old owner John painstakingly uncovers the jacuzzi and prepares a buffet of cocktail sausages, dips and crisps, while the manager, Chantelle, puts up heart-shaped decorations; the club also hosts regular themed evenings such as Mature Mischief on Wednesdays. The film then follows several guests as they pack their lingerie and sex toys for the night and talk candidly to the camera about their lives. Siobhan, 67 and single, enjoys a joyful sex life through swinging and has a playroom of her own. Justin and Hannah, who have been swinging at home for two years, are visiting the club for the first time. Simon and Carolyn, a couple who have swung for four years and feel it strengthens their connection, are dismayed by the poor grammar of some messages on swinging apps. Malika, a single mother and lap dancer, says she has not met a decent man in thirty years, and Martyn turned to the scene after a bad break-up. Interviews touch on difficult episodes in some of the guests' pasts, and the film also shows the morning-after clean-up, as staff deal with what has been left behind.

Reviewers welcomed its candour. Barbara Speed of the i called it a pleasingly banal, human look at British swinging rather than a display of glamour, though she found the interviewer's repeated questions about whether guests were looking for love irritating, concluding that the real taboo was the idea that people might enjoy swinging for its own sake. Rhiannon Evans of Grazia hailed it as the best documentary of 2020, noting that it caused a stir on social media and praising its warm, sympathetic and non-judgemental approach.

At an American university, Professor Annie Holzer (Quick) and Dr. Daniel Barron (Spear) are told by their dean (Hagon) to boost the department's flagging finances with a study of Margam Castle in Wales, a place he doubts they have even heard of. They assemble a team of parapsychologists and cross the Atlantic, encountering superstitious locals and cultural differences before arriving to spend the night in the castle. The historian Hugh Morgan (Nesbitt) supplies its history and the psychic Edith Withers (Merrow) her expertise, but the researchers soon find themselves trying to survive the ghostly figures that inhabit the building, drawn from the castle's legends of a gamekeeper and children in Victorian clothing, as messages appear on mirrors and a sinister little girl haunts them.

In an interview with The Schlock Pit, Jones said that his producing partner Rob Graham suggested the castle after a ghost walk there, and that the building offered a level of production value far beyond his earlier films. Influenced by Pete Walker's House of the Long Shadows and Hammer films, he cast Munro, Merrow and Matheson because they had appeared in Hammer productions, and praised the cast for enduring cold November night shoots and cinematographer Jon McLaughlin for capturing the Gothic atmosphere with limited lighting. The Schlock Pit called it an admirable British horror film in which the castle is the star. Richard E. Rock, a novelist who lives near the castle, was less impressed, finding the story thin, the characters dull, the performances wobbly and the clichés plentiful, but praised Nesbitt and the beautifully shot location and called it an interesting curio.

Susumu Nakoshi (Ayano), a 34-year-old amnesiac, lives in his car between a luxury hotel and a park full of homeless people in western Shinjuku. He is approached by Manabu Ito (Narita), an eccentric medical student, who offers him 700,000 yen to undergo trepanation, drilling a hole in his skull, which is supposed to awaken a sixth sense. After the operation, Nakoshi finds that when he closes one eye he sees the people around him in grotesque, surreal forms. Ito theorises that these visions are homunculi, images of each person's hidden psyche shaped by their deepest trauma. Nakoshi begins confronting the people he sees, among them a feared yakuza boss (Uchino), whose cruelty stems from a childhood accident with a sickle, and a high-school girl known only by the number 1775 (Ishii). Each time he helps someone face their trauma, he takes part of their homunculus onto himself. He also keeps encountering a woman (Kishii) whom he believes to be Nanako, his girlfriend from before his amnesia. He eventually sees her true self and realises she is not Nanako but a woman linked to the car accident that killed Nanako and robbed him of his memory. Recovering his past, he remembers that Nanako had suffered a miscarriage and that she ran into the path of a car during a bitter argument with him. Accepting his guilt, Nakoshi lets the woman go and leaves the experiment behind. He also exposes Ito's own trauma involving his father, and Ito, losing his sanity, drills into his own skull and sews an eye shut so that he can see homunculi himself.

The film departs significantly from the manga, adding Nakoshi's amnesia and Nanako's death and reworking Ito's arc. Reviews were largely negative: The Asian Cinema Critic gave it 4.5 out of 10, praising some ideas and visuals but calling it overlong and weighed down by exposition, though Ayano's performance was generally praised.

Emma and Mia have recently lost their mother, and their father has lost his job in Chicago, so the family moves to the country home where their mother grew up to live with Grandma Rose and help on her ranch. Rose is fading and losing her memory, but her joyful, eccentric spirit revives as she sets the girls to work on the chores. The sisters face bullies at their new school, and at the local general store they meet Willie, a conspiracy-minded local who tells Bigfoot stories and recognizes in Mia a fellow believer. In the woods, Mia spots a sparkling unicorn colt bathed in rainbow light, names him Rocco and discovers the good luck he brings, but no one else can see him and her skeptical father laughs off her claims. Mia researches unicorn lore to prove they exist, and when the more practical Emma finally starts to believe, she too can see Rocco; the sisters even take him to school to deal with a bully. Willie, however, knows the legends as well, and when he learns of Rocco's presence he sets out to capture the colt, intending to kill him and drink his blood to gain eternal youth. When Rose falls ill and is taken to hospital, she pulls out her tubes to help her granddaughters chase down the unicorn-napper, rescue Rocco and return him to his mother.

Reviewers found it a gentle film for young children. Barbara Shulgasser-Parker of Common Sense Media called it sweet and perfectly tailored to its target audience, with smart, amusing dialogue and a charming performance from Webb, though loose in its logic. Roger Moore of Movie Nation described it as cutesy, corny and little-kid friendly, a lightweight cross between Prancer and E.T. with modest effects but enough goofy gags and one-liners to avoid being insipid, while noting it was too undemanding for anyone over eight.

George and Ted travel west by train to Ted's cousin Ginny's farm, having promised to look after it while she goes on vacation with her adventurous mother. Ted, however, knows nothing about farms and little about country life, and the place is run day to day by Emmett, a young farmhand and would-be cowboy who is still learning the ropes himself. George's curiosity and antics quickly upend the farm's routine, and when a runaway wagon rolls down a hill and smashes the corrals, the animals escape and scatter into the countryside.

Despite his inexperience, Emmett keeps his head and organizes a roundup, and the three set off to bring home every last cow, sheep and even a llama. Their trek takes them across a rickety old covered bridge and a wide river, where Emmett rescues a sheep and a dog swept away on a log, and they must flee a shelter threatened by a flash flood. Emmett practices lassoing again and again until he masters it, and his perseverance inspires the cautious Ted to try fishing and horseback riding and George to learn the harmonica. Meanwhile, Ginny finds a similar freedom from her own cautiousness on her trip. By the end, every animal is accounted for and the friends have all gained new skills.

The film premiered exclusively on the streaming service Peacock on 8 September 2020, alongside the arrival of the Curious George television series on the platform, and was released on DVD and digital on 15 December 2020. Common Sense Media described it as a gentle preschool adventure with mild peril and a positive message about being open to new experiences and trying new things.

In a prologue, Helen Modig (Marshall), devastated by the death of her ten-year-old son Jason at the Saint Germaine Children's Clinic, curses a trunk of toys and leaves it on the building's doorstep; on Christmas morning all the other children at the clinic are found dead. Years later, house flipper Hannah Cashman (Teresa) buys the mountainside property to renovate with her contractor Emmett (Pitts), and brings her husband David (Ade), his 15-year-old daughter Alicia (Marks), her young children Zoe (Fish) and Franklin (Elias) and their nanny Rose (Waters) to spend Christmas there. Zoe and Franklin find the trunk, which holds a plush bee, a dinosaur helmet that distorts the wearer's voice, a remote-control car, action figures, a fez-wearing doll called Uncle Monkey and a retro video game console. The younger children begin behaving strangely as the toys sing and dance for them in secret, while Alicia and Rose, who is still haunted by a miscarriage, glimpse the ghost of a little boy. Alicia nearly chokes as Franklin watches, and her video game mirrors events in the house. On Christmas Eve the bee lures Emmett into the attic, where he falls through the floor and is impaled; David is injured in a crash while driving him to hospital. The toys wreck the living room, Uncle Monkey starts a fire, and Christmas decorations attack Hannah until Alicia fights them off. The toys then try to persuade Zoe and Franklin to jump from the attic window to join the dead children. Hannah stops them and Rose helps Alicia lock the toys back in the trunk, but Uncle Monkey stabs Rose, who falls to her death. With David back, the family burn the trunk and leave, while Rose's ghost becomes a kindly carer for the dead children.

Critics found it pleasant but slight. Meagan Navarro of Bloody Disgusting called the stop-motion toys surprisingly charming and the film full of heart, though never scary, with a thin mythology and stilted script. Culture Crypt found it competently made but generic.

Set between the third and fourth seasons, the film follows Marinette Dupain-Cheng and her Parisian classmates on a school trip to New York for French-American Friendship Week. Marinette persuades Adrien Agreste's overprotective father, Gabriel, to let him come along, unaware that Gabriel, secretly the villain Hawk Moth, has his own reasons to travel: a Miraculous has surfaced in New York, an ancient eagle talon he hopes will help him revive his wife. On the flight the students are attacked by the technology-stealing villain Techno-Pirate and rescued by the United HeroeZ, the city's openly public superheroes, among them Majestia, the vigilante Knightowl, his rebellious young protégé Sparrow and the artificial intelligence Uncanny Valley. When Hawk Moth akumatises Techno-Pirate, Ladybug and Cat Noir must join forces with their American counterparts, who are not powered by Miraculouses, while Marinette struggles with her lingering feelings for Adrien.

Critics generally regarded it as an enjoyable outing for fans. Craig Holton of What The Craggus Saw called it slickly animated, wholesomely adventurous and full of invention, a successful leap to feature length that expands the show's mythology, though it offers little help to newcomers. Frédéric Bègue of Chronique Disney praised the comedy and drama between Ladybug and Cat Noir, the new heroes and the action scenes, but found the villain forgettable, the returning supporting characters sidelined and the rushed ending in need of more scenes. Marley Crusch of Bubbleblabber gave it 6 out of 10, deeming it a kids' superhero film that breaks no new ground but is worth watching.

Zeros and Ones is a 2021 thriller written and directed by Abel Ferrara and shot in Rome, the director's adopted home, during the COVID-19 lockdown. Ethan Hawke stars in a dual role as JJ, an American soldier, and his twin brother, with Cristina Chiriac, Phil Neilson, Valerio Mastandrea, Dounia Sichov, Babak Karimi, Stephen Gurewitz and Ferrara's daughter Anna in supporting parts. Developed from an older Ferrara script idea about the post-9/11 war on terror, it was produced by Maze Pictures, Rimsky Productions and Almost Never Films, with cinematography by Sean Price Williams; cast and crew worked in masks and social bubbles, and masks, hand sanitizer and video calls appear on screen.

The film opens and closes with Hawke speaking directly to the audience as himself about the picture. In the story, a gaunt, bearded JJ arrives in a deserted, locked-down Rome on a murky undercover mission, called there to stop an imminent terrorist bombing. He is desperate for news of his twin brother, a messianic revolutionary who is being held captive and tortured and whose fate shifts with each unreliable witness; the brother, glimpsed in brief scenes, rants about fascism and asks why no one sets themselves on fire anymore. Moving through the city at night with armed soldiers and foreign agents on his trail, JJ exchanges terse instructions with strangers in black cars, holds cryptic conversations in a mosque, shares a fraught intimacy with a young mother and her child and buys drugs in a seedy club.

His shadowy errands finally come together when he is caught up in a massive bombing of the Vatican, apparently a staged false-flag operation designed to inflame an ancient conflict between rival civilizations, while the film's dialogue repeatedly casts Jesus as a radical soldier and war casualty. It ends on a hopeful note, with footage of Anna Ferrara running through Rome at sunrise as life returns to the city.

The film opens with Annick (Umuhire) reading from the journal in which she recorded the days spent in hiding. As the violence between Hutu and Tutsi engulfs Rwanda in April 1994, four women take refuge in the storage basement under the kitchen of the house Annick, a pregnant moderate Hutu, shares with her husband Francois (Chirisa), who supplies them with rations and news from outside. With her are Mutesi (Koleosho), a young and angry Tutsi woman who blames the Hutu for the killings; Jeanette (Bingwa), a nun whose faith is repeatedly tested; and Peyton (Cannon), an American on a Peace Corps-style mission who hopes to atone for past sins. At first the women distrust and clash with one another, and at one point Mutesi spitefully eats more than her share of the food. As they share their histories of miscarriage, rape and family strife, Mutesi admits that she does not want to die with her anger, and a sisterhood begins to form. The women draw portraits of one another, learn to read English and become devoted to Seeds of Love, Trees of Peace, a children's book Peyton carries in her bag, while they must stifle their cries as they hear people being executed outside. Over the weeks they suffer nightmares, hallucinations and suffocating conditions. Closing title cards note the role of women in Rwanda's post-genocide recovery.

Hayley is a perfectionist Manhattan event planner who works hard but is still waiting for a long-overdue promotion and keeps fretting about a co-promotion that is on the cards. For the first time in many years she accepts an invitation to spend Christmas with her sister Amy and Amy's new in-laws at the family's holiday home, on one condition: that Paul, the brother of Amy's husband, will not be there. Hayley has a bad history with him from Amy's wedding, holding a grudge against him for ending her last relationship. To everyone's surprise, Paul unexpectedly shows up, though only for one night, or so Hayley thinks until his flight to a ski trip in Switzerland is cancelled the next morning. Forced to spend the days before Christmas together, the two clash, but Paul draws her into a series of holiday activities and recruits her to help the committee planning the town gala, where she takes charge of ticket sales. Hayley, who usually eats only greens and protein, is surprised by how much she enjoys the ribs at the local diner, and she gradually gets the emotionally guarded Paul to open up and embrace the family's Christmas food traditions. As Paul encourages her to stop selling herself short at work, she realizes she may have judged him too quickly, and after a late setback in their relationship he apologizes, showing her that she deserves better in both her career and her love life.

Reviews were mixed. Alakananda Bandyopadhyay of MEAWW found the romance a gush of warmth, praising the leads' ease in their roles and Barbarash's festive direction while finding the score too cartoonish. Rissi JC of RissiWrites enjoyed it as a fun enemies-to-lovers comedy with good banter between Lowndes and Murray, while noting the spark was weaker at the turning point. Jesse Burleson of Views on Film gave it one and a half stars, calling it a predictable slog and finding Murray mostly annoying.

After opening with an older Kitano about to step on stage, the film flashes back to the early 1970s. Kitano, a university dropout, works as an elevator boy and general dogsbody at the France-za, a burlesque theater in Tokyo's Asakusa district whose shrinking audience cares more about the strippers than the comedians performing skits between their routines. The venue is run by Fukami, a famous old-school vaudevillian known for his dapper style and his contempt for the new manzai comedy duos making their names on television. Fukami at first gives the eager newcomer a hard time, then agrees to train him in comedy and tap dance, insisting that he keep an entertainer's mindset not only on stage but in everyday life. Kitano befriends Chiharu, a straight-talking stripper whose dreams of a singing career are behind her, and spends his youth among other gifted, eccentric apprentices as television draws audiences away from the theater. As Kitano's ambition outgrows the failing France-za, he leaves to form the manzai duo Two Beat with Kiyoshi and rises to stardom, while Fukami and his loyal wife Mari face growing misfortune. The film ends with the older Kitano walking through the neighborhood and theater where he learned his craft.

Asakusa Kid was released on Netflix on 9 December 2021. In Variety, Richard Kuipers described it as a safe, traditional and enjoyable biopic that offers little penetrating insight into Kitano but a respectful, touching portrait of Fukami, noting a slowish first half and praising its flights of fantasy, such as Fukami's tap routine and Chiharu's dream of being a torch singer. He called Yagira, a former best actor winner at Cannes, excellent in capturing Kitano's timing and tics, and Oizumi funny and dignified. Other critics similarly praised the leads while finding it conventional and more nostalgic than revealing.

Brenner Baker (Hollman), a decorated Army Ranger, is happily married to Dillon (Passmore), a police detective who still bears the physical and psychological scars of a violent incident involving masked men. Hoping to escape the stress of their jobs, the couple take a road trip into the backwoods of Alabama. Along the way they are harassed by a belligerent local in a pickup truck, and when they run into him again at a diner they learn that he is Butch (Kasper), whose seemingly kindly mother, known as Mama (Singer), defuses the confrontation and lets them leave unharmed. Later, out hiking, the couple are caught in the rain and take shelter in an apparently empty, secluded cabin, only to discover a hidden store of drugs and guns belonging to Butch's family, a criminal clan tied to a cartel and involved in drug dealing and human trafficking. They are captured and interrogated, and both are shot, but the gang fails to check whether Brenner is dead before dumping her in an open grave. Wounded and grieving, she climbs out and uses her combat and survival skills to hunt down the family one by one, while also trying to free other prisoners they hold captive.

Reviews were mixed. Eoin of The Action Elite called the film a slick and effective action picture with a star-making turn from Hollman, who performed her own stunts, including a one-shot fight sequence reportedly rehearsed for only an hour and filmed in a single take; he found the villains so hateful that their comeuppance was satisfying, while conceding that the story was nothing new. Andrew Stover of Film Threat gave it 5 out of 10, writing that its rapid action sequences enliven an otherwise uneven and insipid revenge tale, that its bloody, hammy and clichéd antics fall short of the genre's best, and that Dillon's traumatic backstory is left unexplored.

Most of the performance footage was filmed at Grande's show at the O2 Arena in London. The concert portion runs through a 25-song set list, opening with "Raindrops (An Angel Cried)" and "God Is a Woman" and including "Bad Idea", "Break Up with Your Girlfriend, I'm Bored", "R.E.M.", "7 Rings", "Breathin", "Needy", "NASA", "Into You", "Dangerous Woman", "Break Free" and "No Tears Left to Cry", before closing with "Thank U, Next". Between songs the film cuts to candid moments away from the stage, showing Grande with her dancers, band and crew such as Scott and Brian Nicholson, as well as rehearsals, preparations and casual conversations on the road, presenting a playful and affectionate side of the singer and her team.

The special follows Peter Quill (Star-Lord), Gamora, Drax, Rocket Raccoon, and Groot as they embark on a mission to find a rare and powerful artifact known as the "Orb". This Orb has the power to grant wishes, but it's also extremely difficult to locate. The Guardians are hired by a wealthy client to retrieve the Orb for him.

However, things take a turn when they discover that the Orb is actually a Christmas-themed gift from an unknown benefactor. As they try to figure out who sent the gift and what their intentions are, they begin to experience strange visions of Christmas past, present, and future.

Throughout the special, we see flashbacks of Peter's childhood on Morag, where he was raised by his mother Yondu (who is also a key character in the Guardians of the Galaxy franchise). We also see glimpses of Gamora's troubled past and her complicated relationship with her father Thanos.

As the story unfolds, the Guardians begin to realize that the true meaning of Christmas is not about material gifts or power, but about family, friendship, and giving. They come together to help each other and find a way to make the most of their holiday season.

The special features many Easter eggs and references to the larger Marvel Cinematic Universe, including cameos from characters like Mantis and Nebula. The story is full of humor, heart, and action, making it a fun and festive addition to the Guardians of the Galaxy franchise.

Overall, The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special is a delightful and entertaining holiday special that explores themes of family, friendship, and the true meaning of Christmas. It's a must-watch for fans of the Guardians of the Galaxy franchise and anyone looking for a fun and festive holiday treat.

As the story unfolds, the protagonist undergoes a transformation from a solitary figure to one who begins to connect with those around him. He starts to see the world through the eyes of others, including the young girl and her family, and discovers that even the most unlikely individuals can bring joy and light into each other's lives.

The film also explores the idea of second chances and finding redemption in unexpected ways. The protagonist's journey is not just about changing his own life but also about bringing people together and creating a sense of community. Through his interactions with others, he learns to let go of his gruff exterior and find a softer side, one that allows him to connect with those around him on a deeper level.

Ultimately, A Trash Truck Christmas is a story about the power of kindness, compassion, and understanding in bringing people together during the holiday season. It's a reminder that even in the most unexpected places, joy and love can be found, and that everyone deserves a second chance to experience the magic of Christmas.

The film begins with the rise of powder cocaine as an expensive party drug associated with money, power and glamour, popularised by Richard Pryor's 1980 freebasing accident and by Scarface (1983). As supply boomed and prices fell, by 1984 cocaine was reaching working-class neighbourhoods as crack, a smokable form that gave a short, intense high for the price of a child's allowance. Former dealers describe the trade as a gold rush in neighbourhoods where legitimate work paid little, while turf wars turned streets into battlegrounds and addiction tore families apart, hitting women and mothers especially hard. Pegues recounts being stopped by police with 300 vials and released because dealers were paying off officers. The documentary then turns to the Reagan administration's war on drugs and Nancy Reagan's "Just Say No" campaign, the media's exaggerated coverage of so-called crack babies, and the portrayal of users as overwhelmingly Black when, as the film notes, about two-thirds were white, and it traces the punitive sentencing and militarised policing that swelled the prison population under successive presidents.

Owen Gleiberman of Variety called the film eye-opening, praising Nelson's flair for making history more interesting than the myths it dismantles and its account of how government and media turned crack against the communities it victimised. The New York Times described it as a brisk look back at the crisis, while some critics felt it covered too much ground too quickly to explore every issue in depth.

Richie believes he is the biggest name in Dutch hip-hop, complete with fur coats, a platinum grill and a neck tattoo, and is preparing for his first big arena tour. He is surrounded by an entourage that includes a camera crew filming content for social media, his best friend and hanger-on Tonie (Kolf), his volatile, hard-drinking mother Els (Minis) and his harried manager Jessica (Wong-Loi-Sing), who has just secured him a three-album record deal. Behind the bravado, Richie still seeks his mother's approval and neglects Anna (Kavus), his girlfriend and the mother of his baby son. One night he and Tonie are attacked in a car park by masked youths on scooters, who beat Richie, steal his prized expensive watch and film the assault. When the footage of the rapper in tears goes viral, his carefully built tough-guy reputation collapses and the online mockery threatens his career. Determined to recover the watch and regain control of the story, Richie and Tonie set off on a chaotic hunt for the attackers over the course of one night, a battle fought as much on social media as on the streets, while the thieves begin leaking private material from his phone, including a sex tape with Anna. In the process Richie is forced to confront his own insecurity, the fickle nature of online fame and what he has lost.

Reviewing it for Decider, which recommended streaming it, the critic compared its tension to the Safdie brothers' Good Time and the Polish Netflix film The Hater, describing a frantic film that seems built from the TikTok posts and video calls that punctuate it, and singled out Kavus for bringing real gravity to Anna. De Volkskrant gave it three stars out of five, praising how skilfully Smulders lets a vulnerable boy show through behind Richie's macho exterior. Other Dutch reviewers praised Smulders's energetic performance and the film's satire of social media but found the plot rushed and the characters thinly developed.

A decade after their first case, Ousmane is a commander in the Paris criminal brigade, and after a viral video of him fighting a suspect he is pushed to front a national police recruitment campaign, while François, a captain in the 12th arrondissement, is criticized by colleagues for getting in the way of investigations. The two meet again by chance when François finds half of a corpse on a high-speed train. The victim, Kevin Marchal, came from Valergnes, a town in the Alps, and Ousmane travels there to escape the campaign, with François tagging along. With help from local officer Alice, they learn Kevin was shot off his motorbike onto the tracks and had been running a drug lab in his mother's house. A brawl in a strip club with a bouncer who seems immune to pain, and the man's sudden death, lead them to a security firm whose guards share the tattoo of a militia, the Sons of Clovis. Commissioner Mercier quickly closes the case, but Ousmane refuses to leave. A friend of Kevin's reveals that the victim feared the militia and had asked Mercier for protection.

Following Mercier, the duo is threatened by Brunner, the town's far-right mayor, and attacked on the road. In Brunner's basement they discover plans for coordinated attacks on mosques, synagogues and a migrant center, carried out by fighters taking pain-numbing methamphetamine. In the final showdown, François distracts the militia while Ousmane sabotages their weapons and fights Alice, who turns out to be Brunner's ally. The pair stop a bomb at the migrant center and arrest Brunner and Alice, and François ends up as the face of the recruitment campaign.

Filmed in spring 2021 in Paris and the Alps, the film was released on Netflix on 6 May 2022 and logged more than 78 million hours viewed in its first 28 days. French reviews were mixed: Ouest-France praised the chemistry of Sy and Lafitte, while Les Inrockuptibles felt its political satire and action scenes were less successful than its comedy.

Sam (Deidrick), a commercial photographer in Los Angeles, meets Tara (Drori), a mysterious drifter who lives in vacant houses and seems to have plenty of money from uncertain sources, at an open house. The two share an instant, intensely physical connection, and Tara is soon living in the run-down family home Sam inherited from his parents, renovating it in exchange for a place to stay. As they fall ever deeper in love and race through the milestones of a relationship towards marriage, Sam's business partner and longtime best friend Esther (Elise) worries that they are moving far too quickly, but he ignores her. Tara then reveals that an ex-boyfriend is stalking her, break-ins follow, and Sam's health begins to deteriorate for reasons no one can diagnose, with piercing earaches and moments of disorientation. In its final act the film reveals that Sam, not Tara, is the one in danger, and their consuming romance turns into a tale of transformation and aquatic body horror.

Critics found the film underpowered. Matt Donato of /Film gave it 5 out of 10, writing that its first forty minutes hazily build a relationship between thinly written characters, that Aranovich's attempts at style, such as a fast-motion sex montage and distorted camera views, were not enough, and that its tentacled horror arrives only after the viewer's attention has waned, though he did not fault the performers. Drew Koenig of Tell-Tale TV credited the film with subverting the familiar story of a woman endangered by an untrustworthy man by revealing Sam as the victim of a different kind of toxic love, but felt that Tara's characterisation and the final twist muddied its romantic metaphor and that, while decently paced, it lacked teeth.

Monika Grabarczyk (Chlebicka) is a devoted primary-school teacher, beloved by her pupils though disliked by her demanding, test-obsessed principal (Karolak). Early each morning, however, she swaps her glasses and ponytail for a curly wig, blue contact lenses and glamorous clothes to work as Klaudia, a mysterious model on billboards across the city who only works before nine. She hates modelling and keeps it secret, believing no school would tolerate it, but needs the money to pay off the debts her widowed mechanic father (Baka) owes to loan sharks; he knows nothing of it and only laments that she is not in love. Stefan Tkaczyk (Banasiuk), known to the world as Enzo, is a shallow, womanising model who loves the sports cars he gets to borrow and lives with his boss and lover Alicja (Żulewska) in an open relationship. Their first meeting goes badly when he picks Klaudia up after her car breaks down on the way to a shoot and mistakes her for a prostitute. When Alicja throws Enzo out, he moves in with his brother, whose wife has left the family, and has to look after his young niece Ania (Mazur), who turns out to be one of Monika's pupils. Cast together in an advertising campaign, Enzo feels a spark with Klaudia on set while also being drawn to Monika on school trips, unaware that they are the same woman, while her double life grows ever harder to keep hidden.
